From Checkout Lines to Cooking Classes: Retail Reinvents Itself

Walk into Hartwell & Finch, a department store in downtown Avondale, and you may find a pottery workshop in the homewares section or a wine-tasting event near the food hall. Stores that once relied solely on merchandise sales are increasingly using in-store experiences to draw customers who might otherwise shop online. The Quiet Builder: A Profile of Renata Solis

When Renata Solis founded GreenShell Packaging twelve years ago, she worked out of a rented garage with two employees and a single molding machine. Today, the company she leads produces compostable food containers for more than 2,000 restaurants and grocery chains, and it employs over 400 people at plants in Davenport and Kingsbury. Harbor Ferries to Get First Major Upgrade in Twenty Years

MORELAND BAY (Feb. 9) — The Moreland Bay Ferry Service will modernize its aging fleet and terminals under a $95 million plan approved by the regional transit board last week. The service, which carries about 18,000 passengers daily between five waterfront communities and the city center, has operated essentially unchanged since 2006, and several of its vessels are approaching the end of their service lives. Under the plan, four new hybrid-electric ferries will replace the six oldest diesel boats beginning in 2028. Although the new vessels are fewer in number, each carries nearly twice as many passengers, allowing the service to increase total capacity while cutting fuel consumption by an estimated 40 percent. Terminal improvements will include covered waiting areas, real-time arrival displays, and ramps that adjust automatically to tide levels, which will speed up boarding for passengers with bicycles, strollers, and wheelchairs. Commuter advocacy group Bay Riders United praised the investment but urged the board to also extend evening service hours, noting that the last ferry currently departs at 8:40 P.M. Board chair Vincent Osei said a study of expanded hours will be completed by the end of the year.

In an industry known for quick profits, commercial developer Theodore Lam has built his reputation on waiting. The founder of Lamwood Properties, now one of the region's most respected development firms, is famous for holding sites for years until the surrounding neighborhood matures. His best-known project, the Calloway Mills complex, illustrates the approach. Lam acquired the abandoned textile factory in 2014, when the riverfront district had little foot traffic and most investors avoided the area. Rather than building immediately, he spent five years leasing portions of the property at low rates to artists and small workshops, which gradually drew visitors to the district. Only then did Lamwood begin its full renovation, converting the mills into a mix of offices, shops, and apartments that is now fully leased with a waiting list. "Everyone wants to be the last investor into a neighborhood," Lam said in a rare interview. "I would rather be the first, and then be patient." Lam, who grew up above his parents' hardware store, says the experience taught him that districts thrive when small businesses can afford to stay. Accordingly, every Lamwood project reserves 15 percent of its commercial space for local independent businesses at below-market rents.

For decades, novels translated from other languages occupied a quiet corner of the book trade, accounting for barely 3 percent of fiction sales. That corner is getting crowded. New figures from the Bookscan Literary Index show that sales of translated fiction rose 28 percent last year, the fourth straight year of double-digit growth, with readers under 35 driving most of the increase. Booksellers point to several causes. Literary prizes have raised the visibility of translators, who now frequently appear on book covers alongside authors. Social media reading communities have championed novels from Korea, Japan, and Latin America, sometimes propelling decade-old titles onto bestseller lists. And a wave of small publishing houses devoted to translation has widened the selection available in bookstores. Dorothea Quint, who founded the translation-focused press Meridian Editions nine years ago, says the change is generational. "Younger readers simply do not regard a translated book as foreign," she said. "They follow stories, not borders." Major publishers are responding: at least three large houses have launched translation imprints in the past two years, and advances paid for translation rights have reportedly tripled for sought-after titles. Quint welcomes the competition, saying it benefits translators most of all.
